day-07/acta-sanctorum-tag-der-rueckkkehr.summary: A brief commentary on the feast of the Return of the Child Jesus from Egypt, celebrated on January 7 in the Roman and other martyrologies. The entry surveys variant dates proposed by different liturgical sources.

day-07/0001-acta-sanctorum-julianus.summary: Commentary on St. Julian, Martyr, celebrated January 7. The Bollandists discuss two candidates: one claimed as Bishop of Toledo via the dubious Chronicle of Dexter, and another whose relics were discovered at Cagliari in Sardinia in 1615, venerated throughout the island as 'Sanctu Julianu Conti.'

day-07/acta-sanctorum-spolicostus-pallad.summary: Brief notice of the martyrs Spolicostus, Pallada, and Candida, recorded in the ancient Martyrology of St. Jerome as having suffered in Greece. Nothing further is known of them.

day-07/acta-sanctorum-crispinus-i-von-pa.summary: St. Crispinus I, Bishop of Pavia (ca. 248), succeeded Bishop Ursicinus and governed for thirty-four years under the Emperor Severus. He was known for civic works including paving the city's streets and building a stone bridge over the Ticinus, and for reconciling quarreling citizens.

day-07/acta-sanctorum-felix-und-januariu.summary: Commentary on the martyrs Felix and Januarius, celebrated at Heraclea. The Bollandists debate which Heraclea is meant -- Lucania, Spain, or elsewhere -- and distinguish them from similarly named martyrs venerated on other days.

day-07/acta-sanctorum-polyanthus-philo-u.summary: Brief notice of the martyrs Polyanthus, Philo, and Candida, known only from the Martyrology of St. Jerome. Their place and date of martyrdom are unrecorded.

day-07/0006-acta-sanctorum-julianus.summary: Commentary on a second St. Julian, Martyr in Gaul, whose body rests in a priory of St. John on the Loire in the territory of Anjou. He is distinguished from the Sardinian Julian treated in the preceding entry.

day-07/acta-sanctorum-senator-von-verona.summary: St. Senator, Bishop of Verona, held office between Saints Proculus and Probus, reportedly under the Emperors Diocletian and Maximian (late 3rd century). He is praised for holiness, learning, and gravity; his body was deposited in the basilica of St. Stephen.

day-07/acta-sanctorum-lucian-von-antioch.summary: St. Lucian, Priest of Antioch and Martyr (d. 312), was renowned for his scriptural scholarship and the 'Lucianic' recension of the Bible. After defending orthodox faith against Sabellianism, he was martyred at Nicomedia under Maximinus and buried at Helenopolis in Bithynia. The entry includes extensive discussion of his orthodoxy and his Acts from Metaphrastes.

day-07/acta-sanctorum-clerus-lucerius.summary: St. Clerus (also called Lucerius), Deacon and Martyr at Antioch, was tortured seven times, endured long imprisonment, and was finally beheaded. He is recorded in the Roman Martyrology and numerous other calendars under variant name forms.

day-07/acta-sanctorum-theodorus.summary: St. Theodore, an Egyptian monk who flourished in the time of Constantine the Great (4th century). He was a disciple of St. Ammonius and is mentioned in the lives of Saints Antony and Pachomius, distinct from the Theodore venerated on December 28.

day-07/acta-sanctorum-nicetas-von-dacien.summary: St. Nicetas, Bishop in Dacia (after 401), was an apostolic missionary who rendered fierce and barbarous nations gentle through the Gospel. He visited Italy twice, in 397 and 401, and was warmly praised by St. Paulinus of Nola in his Birthday Poems of St. Felix.

day-07/acta-sanctorum-valentin-von-raeti.summary: St. Valentine, Bishop of Passau (d. ca. 440/482), came from the Germanic Ocean region and evangelized the Rhaetian provinces. Twice visiting Rome for papal support, he combatted both paganism and Arianism at Passau before being expelled and continuing his mission in the Tyrolean Alps, where he died at the castle of Magia.

day-07/acta-sanctorum-crispinus-iii-von-.summary: St. Crispinus III, Bishop of Pavia (d. 466), governed his church for thirty-four years under Popes Sixtus III, Leo I, and Hilarus. He was the mentor and predecessor of St. Epiphanius, who supported him in old age. St. Ennodius praised him in verse.

day-07/acta-sanctorum-valentin-ii-von-te.summary: St. Valentine II, Bishop of Terni (d. ca. 533), was appointed by Pope Gelasius I to the Church of St. Eusebius in Rome before being promoted to the bishopric of Terni, where he converted many Arians and governed for about thirty-nine years.

day-07/acta-sanctorum-cedd.summary: St. Cedd (d. 664), Bishop of the East Saxons and brother of St. Chad, was one of the first apostles to the Middle Angles. Ordained bishop by Finan of Lindisfarne, he evangelized the East Saxons, built churches, and founded monasteries. His life is drawn principally from Bede's Ecclesiastical History.

day-07/acta-sanctorum-tillo-von-solignac.summary: St. Tillo Paul (d. ca. 700), a Saxon by birth, was redeemed from slavery by St. Eligius and trained as a goldsmith and monk at the monastery of Solignac. He accompanied Eligius in evangelizing the Flemish and is venerated as the apostle of Iseghem. His life is given from a Clairmarais manuscript.

day-07/acta-sanctorum-widukind.summary: Blessed Wittekind the Great (d. ca. 807), Duke of the Saxons of Westphalia, led fierce resistance against Charlemagne and Christianity for many years before his conversion and baptism. He thereafter attained great renown for piety and was venerated for miracles after death at Angria near Herford.

day-07/acta-sanctorum-reinold-von-koeln.summary: St. Reinold (date uncertain), monk of St. Pantaleon in Cologne, was reportedly of the Carolingian line. Set over stonemasons by his abbot, he was murdered by them out of envy and cast into a pool. His body was divinely revealed and translated to Dortmund (Tremonia), where the principal basilica bears his name.

day-07/acta-sanctorum-aldrich-von-le-man.summary: St. Aldric, Bishop of Le Mans (d. ca. 856), served as confessor to Emperor Louis the Pious before his episcopal consecration in 832. He built aqueducts, a cloister for canons, and restored churches and monasteries. He was driven from his see by enemies but restored by Pope Gregory IV.

day-07/acta-sanctorum-anastasius-von-sen.summary: St. Anastasius, sixtieth Archbishop of Sens (d. 979), was renowned for holiness, abstinence, perpetual vigils, and generosity. He rebuilt the church of St. Peter at the command of a vision of St. Savinianus. An angel announced his death to his nun sister at the monastery of St. Fara.

day-07/acta-sanctorum-vitalis-von-savign.summary: Blessed Vitalis, Abbot of Savigny (d. ca. 1122), was formerly chaplain to Robert, Count of Mortain. A powerful preacher who spared neither rich nor poor, he founded the monastery of Savigny on the borders of Normandy, Brittany, Maine, and Anjou. His order later adopted Cistercian customs.

day-07/acta-sanctorum-knud-lavard.summary: St. Canute Lavard (d. 1131), Duke of Schleswig and King of the Obotrites, was the nephew of St. Canute the Martyr-King. He governed the Slavic borderlands with virtue and was treacherously murdered by his cousin Magnus. Canonized under Pope Alexander III, his descendants became the kings of Denmark.

day-07/acta-sanctorum-albert.summary: Blessed Albert (d. ca. 1181), hermit of Monte Alceto in the territory of Siena, undertook pilgrimages to Rome, Gargano, Venice, the Holy Land, and Compostela before embracing the eremitical life under the discipline of St. William and the Camaldolese order. He was renowned for miracles including the changing of water to wine.

day-07/acta-sanctorum-raimund-von-pe-afo.summary: St. Raymond of Pennafort (d. 1275), third Master General of the Order of Preachers, was celebrated for learning and holiness. He compiled the Decretals for Pope Gregory IX, co-founded the Order of Mercy for the Redemption of Captives, and was canonized by Clement VIII in 1601. The entry includes an extensive bibliography and a life by Leander Alberti.

day-07/acta-sanctorum-benjamin-und-maxim.summary: Brief notice of the discovery in 1529 at Brescia of the relics of the martyrs Benjamin and Maximus, companions of Saints Faustinus and Jovita. No further details of their lives survive.

day-07/acta-sanctorum-ludwig-von-blois.summary: Louis Blosius (d. 1566), Abbot of Liessies in Belgium, was a prolific spiritual writer whose works -- including the Canon of the Spiritual Life, the Mirror of Monks, and the Psychagogia -- were widely read and approved by the universities of Cologne, Ingolstadt, and Douai. His life was compiled from monastery archives by monks of Liessies.

day-08/acta-sanctorum-semejas.summary: Commentary on the prophet Shemaiah (Semeias), celebrated by the Greeks on January 8. He boldly recalled King Rehoboam from war against the ten rebel tribes and later rebuked him for apostasy when Shishak of Egypt invaded Judah. His prophetic writings, once reckoned among the sacred books, have perished.

day-08/acta-sanctorum-lucian-von-beauvai.summary: St. Lucian, Bishop and Martyr at Beauvais (1st or 3rd century), along with companions Maximian the Priest and Julian the Deacon, evangelized the Bellovaci of Belgic Gaul. Whether he was a companion of St. Dionysius of Paris sent by Pope Clement I, or came later under Diocletian, is debated. According to legend, after beheading he carried his own head to his chosen burial place.

day-08/acta-sanctorum-patiens-von-metz.summary: St. Patiens, fourth Bishop of Metz (d. ca. 152), was a Greek disciple of St. John the Evangelist who received one of the Apostle's teeth as a relic. Sent by John to evangelize Belgic Gaul, he succeeded Bishops Clement, Caelestius, and Felix at Metz. His life is drawn from an ancient manuscript of the Church of Metz.

day-08/acta-sanctorum-anastasius-und-gef.summary: Brief notice of the martyrs of Sirmium in Pannonia: Anastasius, Jucundus, Ratites, Peter, Florus, Tilis, Florian, and Tatia, known from the Martyrology of St. Jerome. Nothing further is established about them.

day-08/acta-sanctorum-claudius-und-gefae.summary: The military martyrs Claudius, Carbonanus, Tibudianus, and Planius suffered at Interamna (Terni) in Umbria under the Emperor Claudius (ca. 270). As garrison soldiers, they supported imprisoned Christians and were themselves seized and martyred.

day-08/acta-sanctorum-maximus-i-ii-von-p.summary: Two bishops of Pavia named Maximus are celebrated on January 8. Maximus I held office around 270 under Emperor Claudius and was praised for his holiness and teachings on the duties of a king. Maximus II, the successor of St. Epiphanius (early 6th century), is praised by Ennodius for his virtue, chastity, and prudent governance.

day-08/acta-sanctorum-patheus.summary: Patheus is known only from the Martyrology of St. Jerome, which records him on January 8 with no further details. He is presumed to be a martyr.

day-08/acta-sanctorum-karterios.summary: St. Carterius, Priest and Martyr in Cappadocia, suffered under Diocletian when the governor Urbanus ruled at Caesarea. He turned his house into a church to instruct Christians, endured horrific tortures including burning, molten lead, and crucifixion, and was finally killed by a Jewish bystander's spear while singing praises in a pyre.

day-08/acta-sanctorum-theophilus-und-hel.summary: Sts. Theophilus the Deacon and Helladius, Libyan martyrs, were savagely beaten, burned, and pierced with potsherds under a proconsul for their confession of Christ. Their Acts are preserved in the Roman Martyrology and Greek Menaea.

day-08/acta-sanctorum-timotheus-und-gefa.summary: Brief notices of the martyrs Timothy, Euctus (or Polyeuctus), Rusticus, and companions, commemorated in Greece. They are known from the Martyrology of St. Jerome and other calendars, but nothing certain is established about their lives.

day-08/acta-sanctorum-eugenianus-von-aut.summary: St. Eugenianus, Martyr at Autun in Gaul, is celebrated on January 8 in the Roman Martyrology and numerous other calendars. He may have been a bishop, though his name does not appear with certainty in the episcopal catalogue. His precise era is unknown.

day-08/acta-sanctorum-egemonius-von-autu.summary: St. Egemonius (or Igonomus), seventh Bishop of Autun, succeeded St. Cassian and is mentioned by St. Gregory of Tours. He flourished in religion and learning and is celebrated on January 8 in numerous martyrologies under many variant name forms.

day-08/acta-sanctorum-atticus-von-konsta.summary: St. Atticus, Bishop of Constantinople (d. 425), initially opposed St. John Chrysostom but later brilliantly atoned through repentance and good works, even persuading St. Cyril of Alexandria to restore Chrysostom's name to the diptychs. He was praised by Pope St. Celestine and the Council of Ephesus for his vigilance against heresy.

day-08/acta-sanctorum-dominica-und-gefae.summary: Sts. Dominica (or Domnica), George the Chozebite, and Aemilian the Confessor are celebrated together from the Greek Menaea. Dominica, born at Carthage, came to Constantinople with four virgins, was baptized by Archbishop Nectarius, and after embracing the solitary life, departed to the Lord around the time of Emperors Leo and Zeno (late 5th century).

day-08/acta-sanctorum-severin-von-noriku.summary: St. Severinus (d. 482), Priest and Apostle of the Noricans, evangelized the Danubian provinces after the death of Attila, renowned for his spirit of prophecy and miracles. His life was written by his disciple Eugippius in 511. His body was later translated to Naples, where it was venerated at the fortress of Lucullanum.

day-08/acta-sanctorum-afflinus.summary: St. Afflinus, Bishop and Confessor, is recorded on January 8 in the Cologne Martyrology and several other calendars. Nothing further has been discovered about him.

day-08/acta-sanctorum-balduin.summary: Blessed Baldwin (7th century), Archdeacon of Laon in Gaul, was the son of Count Alduinus and St. Salaberga. Devoted to Christ from youth and zealous in defending justice, he was murdered by impious men and venerated as a martyr. His life is preserved in a Corsendoncano manuscript.

day-08/acta-sanctorum-maurontus.summary: St. Maurontus, Abbot of Saint-Florent-le-Vieil (Glanna) in Anjou, flourished under King Childebert III (late 7th century). His soul was seen by St. Hermelandus being carried to heaven by angels at the moment of his death.

day-08/acta-sanctorum-frodobert-von-mo-t.summary: St. Frodobertus (d. late 7th century), Abbot and founder of the monastery of Celle (Moustier-la-Celle) near Troyes, was educated under Bishop Ragnegisilus and lived under five bishops of Troyes. Renowned from childhood for miracles -- including restoring his mother's sight -- his relics were translated in 872.

day-08/acta-sanctorum-gudula-gudrun.summary: St. Gudila (d. ca. 712), Virgin and patron of Brussels, was of illustrious Brabantine lineage and trained in piety by St. Gertrude at Nivelles. After Gertrude's death she returned to her father's house and lived a holy life of vigils, prayer, and fasting. Her relics were translated multiple times, ultimately to the church of St. Michael (now St. Gudila's) in Brussels in 1047.

day-08/acta-sanctorum-cyrus-von-konstant.summary: St. Cyrus, Patriarch of Constantinople (ca. 706-714), was a monk near Amastris in Pontus who predicted the recovery of the empire for the exiled Justinian II. Appointed patriarch in gratitude, he likely opposed Monothelitism and facilitated Pope Constantine's historic visit to Constantinople.

day-08/acta-sanctorum-pega.summary: St. Pega (d. after 717), Virgin, was the sister of the hermit St. Guthlac of Croyland. After wrapping his body for burial and re-interring his uncorrupted remains a year later, she eventually set out on pilgrimage to Rome, where she died and was buried. The ringing of all Rome's bells reportedly greeted her arrival.

day-08/acta-sanctorum-erhard-von-regensb.summary: St. Erhard (8th century), Bishop associated with Regensburg, was probably of Irish (Scottish) origin. He evangelized along the Rhine and in Bavaria, and is especially famous for baptizing St. Otilia, who was blind from birth and received her sight. Three separate vitae survive, the earliest by a certain Paulus from the late 11th century.

day-08/acta-sanctorum-gaubald-von-regens.summary: St. Garibaldus (or Gaubaldus), first Bishop of Regensburg (d. ca. 752), was appointed in 739 when St. Boniface divided Bavaria into four dioceses. He translated the relics of St. Emmeram to a new monument with great ceremony. He governed for at least thirteen years.

day-08/acta-sanctorum-wulsin-von-sherbor.summary: St. Wulsinus (d. 983), Bishop of Sherborne, was born in London and became a monk at Westminster. Appointed Abbot by King Edgar through St. Dunstan's patronage, he was later made Bishop of Sherborne under King Ethelred. He predicted the day and hour of his own death and that of his faithful knight Egelwius.

day-08/acta-sanctorum-torphimus-von-hamm.summary: Blessed Torphimus (d. 1284), Bishop of Hamar in Norway, was a Cistercian monk who defended ecclesiastical rights against secular princes and was driven into exile. He died at the Cistercian monastery of Doest (Thosanum) near Bruges; when his tomb was opened decades later, a sweet fragrance filled the church.

day-08/acta-sanctorum-laurentius-giustin.summary: Blessed Laurentius Giustiniani (d. 1455), first Patriarch of Venice, joined the Canons of St. George in Alga at age nineteen and twice served as Prior General, effectively refounding the congregation. Made Bishop of Castello by Pope Eugenius IV and then elevated to the newly created Patriarchate of Venice, he was beatified for his learning, humility, and holiness.

day-09/acta-sanctorum-paschasia.summary: St. Paschasia, Virgin Martyr at Dijon, was instructed and baptized by St. Benignus and suffered martyrdom by fire under Marcus Aurelius (2nd century). Her apparition encouraged builders constructing the basilica of St. Benignus, and an altar was dedicated in her name in 1001.

day-09/acta-sanctorum-epictetus-und-gefa.summary: A group of African martyrs -- Epictetus, Quinctus, Secundus, Jucundus, Saturninus, Vitalis, and others (up to eighteen names) -- are recorded in the Martyrology of St. Jerome and various other calendars. Their Acts have perished and nothing is established about them beyond their names.

day-09/acta-sanctorum-vitalis-und-gefaeh.summary: The martyrs Vitalis, Revocatus, Fortunatus, and companions (Firmus, Possessor, Januarius, Saturninus) are commemorated at Smyrna in the Roman Martyrology and other calendars. Some confusion exists between these and similarly named African martyrs; no Acts survive.

day-09/acta-sanctorum-marciana.summary: St. Marciana, Virgin Martyr at Caesarea in Mauretania, suffered under Diocletian (ca. 300). A native of Rusuccuritana, she smashed a statue of Diana, was tortured, and was finally torn apart by a leopard in the arena. Her Acts survive in multiple manuscripts; the Church of Toledo also claims her.

day-09/acta-sanctorum-julian-und-basilis.summary: Sts. Julian and Basilissa and their numerous companions -- including Celsus, Marcionilla, Antony the Priest, Anastasius, seven boy-brothers, and twenty soldiers -- suffered at Antioch (or Antinous in Egypt) under Diocletian. Their lengthy and miracle-filled Acts, written by a contemporary eyewitness, survive in Greek and Latin. St. Aldhelm and Venantius Fortunatus also celebrate them.

day-09/acta-sanctorum-petrus-von-sebaste.summary: St. Peter, Bishop of Sebaste in Armenia (4th century), was the youngest sibling of Saints Basil the Great, Gregory of Nyssa, and Macrina. Educated entirely by Macrina, he embraced the monastic life, was ordained priest by Basil, and later became bishop. Gregory of Nyssa's Life of Macrina provides the principal testimony to his virtues.

day-09/acta-sanctorum-marcellinus-von-an.summary: St. Marcellinus, Bishop of Ancona, miraculously stopped a great fire that threatened the city by having himself carried to the blaze, which retreated before him. His era is unknown; his story is preserved by St. Gregory the Great in the Dialogues (Book 1, ch. 6). His prayer book, bearing fire marks, was said to heal the sick.

day-09/acta-sanctorum-waningus-von-f-cam.summary: St. Waningus (d. ca. 683), a Frankish nobleman and counselor to King Lothair III, founded numerous monasteries including the convent of the Holy Trinity at Fecamp in Normandy at the direction of a vision of St. Eulalia. He sheltered the exiled St. Leodegarius and was renowned for a miraculous near-death ecstasy in which he saw the rewards of the elect and punishments of the damned.

day-09/acta-sanctorum-filanus.summary: St. Filanus (d. ca. 649), Abbot of Pittenweem in Fife, Scotland, was the son of Feriath and St. Kentigerna. Miraculously preserved from drowning as an infant, he became famous for a luminous left hand that lit his reading and writing at night. His relics were credited with the Scottish victory at Bannockburn in 1314.

day-09/acta-sanctorum-hadrian-von-canter.summary: St. Adrian (d. ca. 709), Abbot in England, was an African-born scholar who declined the Archbishopric of Canterbury, instead recommending Theodore of Tarsus. He accompanied Theodore from Rome to England and served as abbot of the monastery of Sts. Peter and Paul at Canterbury, becoming a renowned teacher of Greek, Latin, and sacred learning.

day-09/acta-sanctorum-bertwald-von-cante.summary: St. Brithwald (d. 731), Archbishop of Canterbury, was formerly Abbot of Reculver. Consecrated in 693 by Godwin, Metropolitan of the Gauls, he governed the English Church for thirty-seven years. He is said to have written a life of St. Egwin of Worcester.

day-09/acta-sanctorum-eustratius-thaumat.summary: St. Eustratius the Wonderworker (d. ca. 9th century), from Tarsia in Bithynia, became a monk at the monastery of Augarus on Mount Olympus. He endured the Iconoclast persecution under Emperor Leo V and was renowned for innumerable miracles. He governed his monastery and died at age ninety-five after a life of extreme asceticism.
